messages.subject: How to deal with missing data in spatial models?
messages.subject_clean: How to deal with missing data in spatial models?
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I'm starting discovering INLA capabilities with simple spatial models and already stumbled upon a problem.

I'm working with individual level data of my study population (120k individuals) distributed over 3000+ spatial units (post code areas).
Each individual has a binary outcome indicating their obesity status, as well as continuous outcome (BMI). Using this data I'm fitting simple binomial and gausian models with 'besag' regional components.

Approximately 100 postcodes have no observation whatsoever. These are legitimate missings since they are located in very sparsely or unpopulated areas.

My question is - how to deal with situation like that?

Shall I compute the graph using all postal code and feed it into inla call? What is happening to the areas where there are no observations?
Or alternatively - shall I compute the graph excluding areas with no observations (changing the structure of 'original' graph with all postal codes of the country)?

radek

messages.body_plain:
On 05/02/14 07:58, Jussi wrote:
> I found that the "user friendly" results and expected values calculated
> from the marginals do not match, for example:
>
> c(exp(spde.result$summary.log.kappa$mean), inla.emarginal(identity,
> spde.result$marginals.kappa[[1]])) # Not the same

Let g(theta) be a linear functional of a vector-valued theta.
Then
exp(E(g(theta)|Y))  is _not_ the same thing as E(exp(g(theta))|Y)
so they _should_ not match.  (And Jensen's inequality says that
the first is smaller than the second, which is precisely what we get.)

> tau <- exp(spde.result$summary.log.tau$mean)
> kappa <- exp(spde.result$summary.log.kappa$mean)
> c(sqrt(8)/kappa, exp(spde.result$summary.log.range.nominal$mean)) # The same

Yes, and here they should match, since both are exp(E(g(theta)|Y)), and
computed in the same way.

> c(1/(4*pi*tau^2*kappa^2),
> exp(spde.result$summary.log.variance.nominal$mean)) # Not the same

Here, you _are_ right that the results should be the same, in theory.

The difference likely occurs due to the skewness of the
distributions;  The error can be expected to be smaller when directly
approximating the distribution for log(variance) than approximating
log(tau) and log(kappa) separately and then summing their respective
expectations, but I'm surprised that the difference seems to be so
noticeable.

Finn L

messages.subject: How to include INLA graphs in knitr LaTeX output?
messages.subject_clean: How to include INLA graphs in knitr LaTeX output?
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I'm trying to figure out how to include INLA graphs in knitr LaTeX output.

The actual code is not relevant here so I used some exemplary code from tutorials to generate minimal example:

# #################################

\documentclass{article}

\begin{document}

<<c1>>=
library("INLA")

n = 100
z = runif(n)
eta = 1 + 0.1*z
N = 20

p = exp(eta)/(1+exp(eta))
y = rbinom(n,  size = N, prob = p)
r = inla(y ~ 1 + z,
         data = data.frame(y, z),
         family = "binomial",
         Ntrials = rep(N, n),
        control.family = list(link = "logit"),
        control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE)
        )
@

<<c2, fig.width=".25\\linewidth" >>=
plot(r, single=TRUE)
@

\end{document}

# #################################

The code runs smoothly and pdf report is produced. However - it does not include graphics.

I posted a question on SO <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/21534751/in-r-and-knitr-how-do-i-plot-inla-results> and solution suggested there was to use

noop <- function(...) NULL
assignInNamespace("inla.dev.new <http://inla.dev.new>", noop, ns="INLA")

That trick includes the graphs but again - breaks some functionality of the knitr package.

Is there any method to overcome this problem?

Hello,

Since I upgraded INLA, I can not fit mixed model in the same way as before.

Code below show how I fit mixed model on two group data. Random effect represent time and Z matrix indicate penalized splines, with two options to have same
(ZSplSame) and different (ZSplDiff) spline per group. If I run code on the old version of INLA give me the attached plot1, where in the first row fitted curve have the same
shape for both groups, while in the second row curves differ per group. After I upgraded INLA same and different splines give identical fit as in the plot2 and also I get warning message.

Could you tell me how to overcome this problem and whether warning message have any impact on estimation of the model.

Best regards,
Viktorian.

ge1 <- c(9,8,5,6,4,5,2,4)
ge2 <- c(8,5,4,7,8,7,10,11)
ge <- c(ge1,ge2)

# Time effect
timefac <- c(rep(1:8, 2))
# Group effect
groupfac <- factor(rep(1:2, each=8))

# Design matrix for random effect (Splines)
ZSpl <- matrix(c(28.51380432,13.83085771,5.32035999,1.29891601,0.08313062,0.01039133,0.66504500,3.56422554,
             3.56422554,0.66504500,0.01039133,0.08313062,1.29891601,5.32035999,13.83085771,28.51380432),8,2)

The first argument is un-named (denoted ... in the help) and it is usually just the name of the effect, i.e. f(<name of covariate>, model= .....).

In the case where there are weights, the un-named argument has the name and the weights and the call is  f(<name of covariate>, <weights>, model=.....)

1) a poisson regression with the number of infected individuals per pixel (unknown) being dependent on the pixel level covariates (known)
2) The number of infected individuals per catchment area (known) being the sum of the unknown number of infected individuals per pixel within the catchment.

I can't work out how to specify this in INLA to estimate the pixel level coefficients. I realise that I may have to account for spatial autocorrelation between catchments (and pixels) down the line but wanted to get a basic model up and running first. Any guidance would be fantastic. I've included some toy code which might help explain my problem better.

Thanks very much,
Hugh

messages.body_plain:
On 18 February 2014 12:59, K.e <eliudk...@gmail.com> wrote:
> In statistics  we have that 68% of values are within 1 standard deviation of
> the  mean , 95% of values are within 2 standard deviation and  of the mean
> and 99.7%  of values are within 3 standard deviation of the mean.

No, that is only true for Normal distributions (and even then your
values are only approximate).

> Questions
>
> 1  Is it possible to  predict standard deviations based on each level using
> INLA ?

I think what you are looking for is _quantiles_, i.e. values defining
intervals containing specified probability masses.
These are computed by INLA, yes.

>  2 I usually use the following code to extract standard deviations
>
>  field_pred_sd <- result$summary.linear.predictor[inla.stack.index(stack,
> "pred")$data, "sd"]
>
>  Can the code be modified to extract  at 1 sd, 2sd and 3 sd.

2sd is trivially obtained by 2*sd, but as I said above, that is almost
certainly not what you are looking for.
Instead of "sd", you can extract quantiles with "0.025quant",
"0.5quant", and "0.975quant" (i.e. by default INLA computes the 0.025,
0.5 and 0.975 quantiles).

To obtain other quantiles, see this quote from on old discussion board
message from 2011:
(I think both methods mentioned still work):

"
you can either add it generally

inla(...., quantiles = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9))

or to extract them afterwards, like

> y=1:10
> r=inla(y~1, data = data.frame(y))
> inla.qmarginal(c(1:10)/11, r$marginals.hyperpar[[1]])

0.11775221799

0.21038705053
"

> two: control.fixed = list(correlation.matrix=TRUE), and control.inla =

> for? fixed effects or lincomb?

The posterior correlation matrix for the fixed effects, is implemented
through linear.combinations, just make one lincomb for each fixed
effect. the option in control.fixed is just a short-hand for this. if
you have additional lincombs, these new ones will be added.

> 2. The following small simulation shows some weird results for me.

> > Sigma #This will be the real covariance matrix
>      [,1] [,2]
> [1,]   10    3
> [2,]    3    2
> > beta <- mvrnorm(n=1000, c(-2,7), Sigma)
> >
> > y = 1 + beta[,1] * x1 + beta[,2]*x2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)
> >
> > formula = y ~ 1 + x1 + x2
> >
> > result = inla(formula,
> +               data = data.frame(x,y),
> +               control.fixed = list(correlation.matrix=TRUE),
> +               family = "gaussian")
> > result$misc$lincomb.derived.covariance.matrix
>             (Intercept)          x1          x2
> (Intercept)  0.02360268   0.2343025  -0.2690078
> x1           0.23430254  97.0017226 -97.0702108
> x2          -0.26900779 -97.0702108  97.2078268
>
>
> I know this may be conceptually wrong, and the beta should be treated
> as random effect rather than fixed.
> How to understand the posterior covariance between fixed effects?  If
> you can get back to me a small example, I will be really appreciate.

yes, you simulate from a model with 'correlated random effects' but
estimate it with fixed effects, so... you can of'course change the model
so its correct according to the data or the oposite.

the 'fixed effects' in the Bayesian context, is just a (Gaussian)
variable with a prior mean and precision, and conditioning on data gives
you the posterior distribution for them and the posterior correlation
matrix is the correlation matrix between these three 'fixed effects',
and so with the covariance matrix.

the phrase 'fixed' and 'random' does not make much sense in the Bayesian
context, as only the prior is different, but we still use the phrase
still. a fixed effect have prior N(0, prec) and both mean and prec are
fixed. a random effect have prior (f.ex) N(0, prec) and prec is random
as well with its own prior.

Note that _quartile_ specifically refers to the 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75 _quantiles_ ("divided into four parts", like a string quartet...).

It is not at all clear what you are actually trying to achieve, since you still confuse quantiles with standard deviations; standard deviation is a precisely defined concept, and so are quantiles, and they are not interchangeable in the way you write, except for specific relations in specific distributions, such as Gaussians. The posterior distributions are not Gaussian, so you need to be more careful.

Thirdly, standard deviation is a measure of spread, whereas a quantile is an absolute value. To measure spread (e.g. Inter quartile range) you need to take the difference between two quantiles, e.g. 0.025 and 0.975 or between 0.75 and 0.25.

 Please explain more carefully what you mean by
classifying the mean map into 3 levels based on quantiles
The mean map is a point estimate of the field.  The 0.5 quantile is also a point estimate of the field (the point-wise medians).  Do you mean that you want to classify the posterior distribution of the field into categories according to the uncertainty somehow?

Dear INLA expert group,
I am quite new to the INLA approach and I've recently started to look at the R-INLA package for an analysis on which I would appreciate your advice and suggestions.

I want to understand if the distribution of a fishing fleet in a certain time period is associated to particular hydrographic conditions which are known to affect the distribution of fish.

_ 1-hour time interval GPS locations (PING) that describe the position of each active vessel in the fleet
_ high resolution raster with hydrographic information (EnvVar) on the whole area
_ high resolution raster with depth information (Depth)

Yes, if EnvVar and Depth are purely functions of location, then all you
need to do is to supply the values corresponding to the integration
points, in this example the triangulation nodes.

(If EnvVar was _not_ a function of location, one would need to expand
the integration to the product space of Location and EnvVar)

However, note that when EnvVar and Depth are pure functions of
location, their effects are not identifiable, since the spatial effect
itself can always be made to capture the other two effects.  The
results are therefore highly dependent on the priors and an linear
constraints imposed to achieve mathematical identifiability. The sum of
the effects can be identifiable without the individual components being
identifiable, and having the two rw2 models present may very well help
to getting a better fit; one just has to be careful when interpreting
the results.
Also note that this problem is not unique to R-INLA, but a fundamental
issue with all such models.

Finn L

On 25/02/14 14:09, Valerio Bartolino wrote:
> Finn, if the effect of the individual components cannot be identify it
> means that I won't go very far in trying to answer my initial question
> in this way, correct?

No, it just means that it isn't as straightforward as simply looking at
the estimated EnvVar effect in isolation, and that you need to be
careful to use appropriate priors and linear constraints.

> Because my main interest is identifying if there is an association with
> EnvVar I want to interpret then the effect of this specific component.
> The reason why I included Depth is because it is a kind of confounding
> effect when studying the distribution of a fishing fleet (an effect I
> want to account for in some way).

Yes, and that is perfectly sensible.  The problem is that _both_ those
effects are confounded with the spatial effect itself.  The severity of
the problem depends on the actual properties of the EnvVar field across
space.  The Depth effect will definitely be highly confounded with the
spatial effect.

> Would the issue of identifiability be solved or less problematic if I
> use for instance a second-order polynom for the effects of EnvVar and Depth?

In the case of linear effects one can sometimes get useful results by
mandating that the spatial effect should be orthogonal to the spatial
covariates (in this case EnvVar and Depth).  For low-order polynomials
that would also work in theory at least, by mandating orthogonality to
the polynomial basis function fields, but I haven't personally tried
doing that.
There is support in inla.spde2.matern() for specifying integral
constraints over the mesh, which is what you would meed for this.

Finn

messages.subject: Geometric anisotropy
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm writing to inquire whether there is documentation for how to implement "geometric anisotropy" in R-INLA and/or the SPDE approach?  Geometric anisotropy is obviously a very frequent model to explore when isotropy fails to explain the data well and, while I see some discussion of general anisotropy and nonstationarity, it would be convenient to have this intermediate level to explore.

Cheers,
Jim

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Geometric anisotropy
messages.body_plain:
Hi James,
Right now we do not have that implemented.

We've written a few papers on it, but the challenge is coming up with a useful parameterisation that has few enough hyperparameters to be useful in INLA.

Conceivably, we could have a model of stationary anisotropy, but we haven't implemented that either.

These papers are listed here: http://arxiv.org/find/stat/1/au:+Fuglstad_G/0/1/0/all/0/1

Best wishes,

Dan

Dan,

At the risk of trying your patience:

do you have an example of how to calculate the precision matrix arising from Eq. 6 of Fuglstad et al. (arXiv) that you linked?

For isotropy, I've previously computed:

Q = kappa^4*G0 + 2*kappa^2*G1 + G2

where:
G0=spde$param.inla$M0
G1=spde$param.inla$M1
G2=spde$param.inla$M2

and feeding the precision matrix Q into other software (i.e. Template Model Builder).  Is there an analogous way to compute Q given the parameterization of geometric anistropy H in that paper and the mesh computed by INLA?

Cheers,
Jim
